idiom_name: compiler-enforced access levels (private, fileprivate, private(set)) plus a single mediating method
implementation_notes: Swift's access levels are enforced by the compiler: private restricts an entity to its enclosing declaration and same-file extensions, fileprivate to the source file, and private(set) makes a property readable but not writable from outside - together they give the mediator a single visible route to its state and stop callers from writing it directly. The classic wrapper is therefore the type itself: a struct or class whose stored properties are private and whose methods perform the policy check before touching them, with private(set) var plus a checked mutator replacing a public setter. The scope difference bites in practice: fileprivate is far broader than private, so helper code placed in the same file can reach the mediator's internals, and @testable import widens internal declarations for test targets - neither should be relied on for enforcement.
pitfalls: fileprivate (and extensions in the same file) exposes the stored properties to any code in that file, so internals are only private while they stay in the declaring declaration.
Value semantics cut both ways: the copy a caller receives after a permitted read is a fully unmediated Record, so return projections rather than the protected value when later use must be covered.
@testable import makes internal declarations visible to test targets; never rely on internal for enforcement, and keep tests from becoming a documented bypass.
For NSObject subclasses KVC/setValue(_:forKey:) can bypass access levels; keep mediated types free of Objective-C runtime exposure where the boundary matters.
